title: The Tower and the Gods of the Nations
bigQuestion: What does the Bible say happened to the nations after Babel, and how did Michael Heiser read it?

story.title: Seventy Names on a Map
story.kicker: Maya counts the nations in Genesis 10 and finds a number that shows up again and again.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz unrolled a big paper map across two desks. It showed the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. It stretched east to the rivers of Iraq. "This is the world the writers of Genesis knew," she said. "Today we will read a list of nations." Maya held a pencil and a stack of sticky notes.

The class opened to Genesis 10. The chapter lists the families that came from Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. Each time Maya read a new name, she wrote it on a note. She stuck it on the map. Some names were easy, like Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. Others, like Tarshish, made the class guess and look things up.

When the list ended, Maya counted her notes. "Seventy!" she said. Ms. Ortiz smiled. "Many readers count seventy in the Hebrew text," she said. "The old Greek translation has a couple more. That number, seventy, shows up in some surprising places."

"Where else?" asked Maya. Ms. Ortiz pointed to the next chapter, Genesis 11, and the tower of Babel. Then she held up the book of Deuteronomy. "A scholar named Michael Heiser thought these chapters fit together," she said. "He thought they explain how the nations began, and who was put in charge of them."
story.think: Why do you think Genesis puts a long list of nations right before the story of the tower of Babel?

lessons.title: One Language, One Plan
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 11 says everyone spoke one language and decided to build a city and a tower that reached toward the sky.
reading: Genesis 11 begins with a picture. The whole earth had one language. People moved east and settled on a plain in the land of *Shinar*. There they made bricks and baked them hard. They used a sticky black tar to hold the bricks together.

Shinar is an old name for southern *Mesopotamia*. That is the land between two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. Today most of it is in Iraq. In the story, the people made a plan there. They would build a city and a tower whose top reached into the sky (Genesis 11:4).

The builders gave two reasons. They wanted to make a name for themselves. They also did not want to be scattered over the earth. Earlier, God had told Noah's family to fill the earth (Genesis 9:1). Many Jewish and Christian readers see Babel as a story about pride. The builders put their own name first.

words.d: an old name for southern Mesopotamia, where the story of Babel takes place
the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, mostly in today's Iraq

look.title: Genesis 11:4 in Simple Words
look.text: The people said to each other: Come, let us build a city and a tower that reaches up to the sky. Then we will be famous, and we will not be scattered all over the earth.
look.cite: Genesis 11:4, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What two things did the builders want? Which one goes against God's words to Noah in Genesis 9:1?

check.q: Where did the builders settle, according to Genesis 11?
choices: On a plain in the land of Shinar
On an island in the sea
check.why: Genesis 11:2 says the people settled on a plain in Shinar, an old name for southern Mesopotamia.

check.q: What did the builders want for themselves?
choices: To build a boat for the animals
To make a name for themselves
To spread out over the whole earth
check.why: Genesis 11:4 says the builders wanted to make a name for themselves and stay together.

check.q: Why do many readers see Babel as a story about pride?
choices: The builders asked God for help
The builders wanted to be famous and stay in one place
The builders wanted to leave the city
The builders were too tired to finish
check.why: The builders put their own name first and did not want to fill the earth, as God had told Noah's family in Genesis 9:1.

lessons.title: God Comes Down
lessons.mainIdea: In the story, God comes down, mixes up the people's language and scatters them, and the city is called Babel.
reading: Genesis 11:5 says the LORD came down to see the city and the tower. The builders wanted to reach up to heaven. Instead, God comes down to them. Many readers notice the gentle joke here. The tower seemed very tall to its builders. Yet God still had to come down to see it.

Then God speaks. In Genesis 11:7, God says, let us go down and mix up their language. Heiser noticed the word us. He thought God was speaking to his *divine council*, the heavenly beings around him. Other readers think us is a royal way of speaking. Some Christians hear a hint of the Trinity.

After that, the people could not understand each other. They stopped building and spread out over the earth. The city was named *Babel*. In Hebrew, that name sounds like balal, a word that means to mix up. Babel is also the Hebrew name for Babylon, a great city of Mesopotamia.

words.d: God's heavenly court: the spirit beings around God's throne, as Heiser described it
the city in Genesis 11; its name sounds like the Hebrew word for mix up, and it is the Hebrew name for Babylon

look.title: Two Readings of Let Us
look.text: Genesis 11:7: God says, Let us go down and mix up their language. Reading A (Heiser): God is speaking to his heavenly council, like a king speaking to his court. Reading B (some other readers): God is speaking in a royal way, the way a king might say we. Many Christians also hear a hint of the Trinity.
look.prompt: Which clue in the verse would each reader point to? Could another verse with us, like Genesis 1:26, help you think about it?

check.q: According to Genesis 11:5, what did the LORD do?
choices: Came down to see the city and the tower
check.why: Genesis 11:5 says the LORD came down to see the city and the tower the people were building.

check.q: Heiser thought the word us in Genesis 11:7 showed God speaking to whom?
choices: His divine council of heavenly beings
check.why: Heiser read us as God speaking to his divine council, the heavenly beings around him.

check.q: The name Babel sounds like a Hebrew word that means what?
check.why: Babel sounds like balal, the Hebrew word for mix up, which is what happened to the people's language.

lessons.title: A Tower Like a Ziggurat
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the tower as a temple-tower meant to bring the gods down, and he called Babel the third rebellion in Genesis.
reading: Archaeologists have found the remains of ziggurats in Iraq. A *ziggurat* was a tall tower built in steps, like a giant staircase. It stood beside a temple. People in Mesopotamia believed a god could come down to the temple there. The great ziggurat of Babylon was called Etemenanki. Its name means temple of the foundation of heaven and earth.

Many scholars think the tower of Babel was pictured as a ziggurat. Heiser agreed. He argued the builders were not only proud. He thought they wanted a place to bring the gods down on their own terms. So he saw Babel as a *rebellion*, a turning away from God. In The Unseen Realm (2015), he called it the third big rebellion in Genesis.

In Heiser's reading, the first rebellion was in Eden, when the serpent tricked Eve. The second was in Genesis 6, when the sons of God did wrong. Babel was the third. Other readers agree that Babel is about pride and turning from God. They may not see it as one of a set of three. Both readings end with people scattered.

words.d: a tall tower built in steps beside a temple in ancient Mesopotamia
a turning against the one in charge; refusing to follow

look.title: Picture a Ziggurat
look.text: Picture a hill made of dried mud bricks, flat on top, rising in wide steps. Each step is smaller than the one below. A long staircase climbs the front. At the very top stands a small shrine. The people below believed their god could come down to this place.
look.prompt: Why might a tower like this remind readers of the tower of Babel, whose top reached toward the sky?

check.q: What was a ziggurat?
choices: A tall stepped tower beside a temple
check.why: A ziggurat was a tall tower built in steps beside a temple in Mesopotamia.

check.q: Heiser called Babel the third rebellion. Which were the first two?
choices: Cain and Abel, and Noah's ark
The call of Abram and the flood
The Exodus and the golden calf
Eden and the sons of God in Genesis 6
check.why: In Heiser's reading, Eden was the first rebellion, Genesis 6 the second, and Babel the third.

check.q: In which book did Heiser lay out his reading of the three rebellions?
check.why: Heiser described the three rebellions in his book The Unseen Realm, published in 2015.

lessons.title: Noah's Three Sons
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 10 lists the peoples who came from Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and scholars call it the Table of Nations.
reading: Genesis 10 is a long list of names. It is often called the *Table of Nations*. It tells which peoples came from each of Noah's three sons: Japheth, Ham and Shem. Many names are people. Many are also names of lands or cities. The list moves from one son to the next.

Each part of the list ends the same way. It says these peoples had their own families, languages, lands and *nations* (Genesis 10:5, 20 and 31). Some names are easy to know. Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Canaan is the land where Israel later lived. Other names, like Tarshish, still puzzle scholars.

The list also names Nimrod, a mighty hunter and king. Genesis 10:10 says his kingdom began in Babel and other cities in Shinar. So Genesis 10 mentions Babel before chapter 11 tells its story. The two chapters are linked. Chapter 10 shows the nations spread out. Chapter 11 then tells a story about why.

words.d: the name scholars give to the list of peoples in Genesis 10
large groups of people who share a land, a language or a family story

look.title: Genesis 10:32 in Simple Words
look.text: These are the families of Noah's sons, listed by their family lines and their nations. From them the nations were divided and spread out over the earth after the flood.
look.cite: Genesis 10:32, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: This verse closes the list. Which words in it point ahead to the story of Babel in Genesis 11?

check.q: What do scholars call the list of peoples in Genesis 10?
check.why: Genesis 10 is called the Table of Nations because it lists the peoples who came from Noah's sons.

check.q: Which name in Genesis 10 is the Hebrew name for Egypt?
check.why: Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Shinar is southern Mesopotamia, and Tarshish is still debated.

check.q: Why is Nimrod in Genesis 10 a link to Genesis 11?
choices: He was the father of Abram
check.why: Genesis 10:10 says Nimrod's kingdom began in Babel, the city whose story comes in Genesis 11.

lessons.title: Counting Seventy
lessons.mainIdea: Readers count about seventy nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10, and seventy came to stand for all the nations.
reading: Readers who count the names in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10 get about seventy. The *Septuagint* has a couple more, about seventy-two. The Septuagint is an old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. Its first books were made in Egypt around 250 BCE. In later Jewish writing, the seventy nations came to mean all the peoples of the world.

The number seventy shows up in Israel's own story too. Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 say seventy people from Jacob's family went down to Egypt. So the world has seventy nations, and Israel begins with seventy people. Many readers think this match is on purpose.

Heiser pointed to another seventy. Clay tablets from *Ugarit*, an old city in Syria, tell of the high god El. His wife Athirat had seventy sons. Heiser thought Bible writers knew this picture of a high god with a family of lesser gods around him. He used it to help explain Deuteronomy 32, which comes later in this chapter.

words.d: an old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt around 250 BCE
an ancient city in Syria whose clay tablets tell stories of the god El and his council

look.title: Nations in Genesis 10, by Son of Noah
look.cite: Genesis 10, Hebrew (Masoretic) text; a common scholarly count
look.prompt: Add the three numbers. What total do you get? Why do readers care about that number?

check.q: About how many nations do readers count in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10?
check.why: The usual count of nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10 is seventy: 14 from Japheth, 30 from Ham and 26 from Shem.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: An old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Septuagint is the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt around 250 BCE.

check.q: What do clay tablets from Ugarit say about the high god El?
choices: He and his wife had seventy sons
check.why: The Ugarit tablets tell of El and his wife Athirat, who had seventy sons. Heiser compared this to the seventy nations.

lessons.title: First the List, Then the Story
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis puts the list of nations before the Babel story, so readers see the result first and then the story of why.
reading: Genesis 10 comes before Genesis 11, but the events are not in that order. Genesis 10 already shows many languages. Genesis 11 begins with one language. So the writer shows the result first. Then he goes back to tell the story behind it. Storytellers still do this today.

Genesis 10:25 gives a clue. It names a man called *Peleg*. It says that in his days the earth was divided. The name Peleg sounds like the Hebrew word for divide. Many readers link this verse to the scattering at Babel. Others think it means something else, such as a dividing of land.

Heiser read Genesis 10 and 11 together with a third passage, Deuteronomy 32:8. That verse also talks about God dividing the nations. To Heiser, the three passages told one story. People were scattered at Babel. Then God did something about the nations. The next section looks at what Heiser thought that was.

words.d: a man in Genesis 10:25 whose name sounds like the Hebrew word for divide
to spread out in many directions; in Genesis 11 the builders are scattered over the earth

look.title: Result First, Story Second
look.text: Imagine a picture book. The first page shows a broken vase on the floor. The next page goes back in time. It shows the cat jumping on the shelf. Genesis 10 is like the first page: the nations are already spread out. Genesis 11 is like the next page: it tells how it happened.
look.prompt: Why might a writer show the result first and tell the story second? Can you think of a book or movie that does this?

check.q: Which detail shows that Genesis 11 goes back in time from Genesis 10?
choices: It begins with the whole earth speaking one language
It tells of Abram leaving Haran
check.why: Genesis 10 already shows many languages, but Genesis 11 begins with one language, so it goes back to tell how the change happened.

check.q: What does the name Peleg sound like in Hebrew?
check.why: Genesis 10:25 says the earth was divided in Peleg's days, and his name sounds like the Hebrew word for divide.

check.q: Which passage did Heiser read together with Genesis 10 and 11?
check.why: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8, which speaks of God dividing the nations, together with Genesis 10 and 11.

sections.title: Moses' Song and the Old Copies

lessons.title: The Most High Divides the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 says the Most High divided the nations and set their borders, and the LORD kept Israel as his portion.
reading: Deuteronomy 32 is a long poem. It is often called the Song of Moses. In the story, Moses teaches it to Israel near the end of his life. The song looks back over Israel's history. Verse 8 looks all the way back to the time the nations were split up.

Verse 8 says the *Most High* gave the nations their *inheritance*. He divided the peoples and set their borders. Verse 9 says the LORD's *portion* is his people. Jacob, another name for Israel, is his share. So the nations get their lands. The LORD keeps one people for himself.

One phrase in verse 8 is hard. It says the borders were set by the number of someone. But whose number? Old copies of the Bible say different things here. Heiser thought this small phrase was a key to his whole reading of the Bible. The next lesson shows the choices.

words.d: a title for God in the Hebrew Bible, meaning the highest one over all
land or goods given to someone to keep, often passed down in a family
a share that belongs to someone; Deuteronomy 32:9 calls Israel the LORD's portion

look.title: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in Simple Words
look.text: When the Most High gave the nations their lands, when he split up the families of people, he set their borders by the number of ______. But the LORD's own share is his people. Jacob is the part he chose for himself.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 32:8–9, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611); the blank marks the words old copies disagree on
look.prompt: The blank is the puzzle of this section. Before you read on, what words do you think might fit there?

check.q: What is Deuteronomy 32 often called?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32 is a poem that Moses teaches Israel, so it is often called the Song of Moses.

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 32:9 call the LORD's portion?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion is his people, and Jacob is his share.

check.q: What does the title Most High mean?
check.why: Most High is a title for God in the Hebrew Bible. It means the highest one over all.

lessons.title: Sons of Israel or Sons of God?
lessons.mainIdea: The standard Hebrew text says sons of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8, but a Dead Sea Scroll says sons of God, and the Septuagint points the same way.
reading: Most printed Hebrew Bibles use the *Masoretic Text*. Careful Jewish scribes called the Masoretes copied it. Its oldest complete copy of the Hebrew Bible, the Leningrad Codex, was made in 1008 CE. In Deuteronomy 32:8, this text says the borders were set by the number of the sons of Israel. The King James Version follows it.

In 1947, people began finding the *Dead Sea Scrolls* in caves near the Dead Sea. Many of the scrolls are more than two thousand years old. One copy of Deuteronomy from these caves says sons of God in verse 8. Many copies of the Septuagint point the same way. They say angels of God or sons of God.

So which reading came first? Many scholars think sons of God is older. They think a later scribe changed it, perhaps to avoid talk of other heavenly beings. Some newer English Bibles now follow the scroll here. Others keep sons of Israel and add a note. Heiser followed the scroll and the Septuagint.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Bible, carefully copied by Jewish scribes called the Masoretes
very old scrolls found in caves near the Dead Sea starting in 1947, including copies of Bible books
a person whose job was to copy writings by hand

look.title: How Old Are the Witnesses?
rows: Septuagint of the Torah first made (c. 250 BCE)
Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy (c. 50 BCE)
look.cite: Common scholarly dates for the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Leningrad Codex
look.prompt: Which witness is oldest? Why might scholars pay close attention to an older copy?

check.q: What does the Masoretic Text say in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: The Masoretic Text, and the King James Version that follows it, say sons of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8.

check.q: Where were the Dead Sea Scrolls found?
choices: In caves near the Dead Sea
check.why: The Dead Sea Scrolls were found in caves near the Dead Sea, beginning in 1947.

check.q: Which reading did Heiser follow in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: Sons of God, as in the Dead Sea Scroll
check.why: Heiser followed sons of God, the reading of a Dead Sea Scroll, with the Septuagint pointing the same way.

lessons.title: Heiser's Reading
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that after Babel God placed the nations under lesser elohim, the sons of God, and kept Israel as his own.
reading: Heiser put the pieces together. At Babel, people turned from God. So, in his reading, God handed the nations over. He set them under the sons of God, lesser *elohim* in his council. He kept one people for himself, Israel. That is why verse 9 says the LORD's portion is his people.

Elohim is a Hebrew word. It can mean God. It can also mean other spirit beings. Heiser said the word tells where a being lives, in the spirit world. It does not mean the being is equal to Israel's God. Heiser argued that the LORD is far above them all, and that he made them.

Heiser also pointed to Psalm 82. There God judges the elohim for being unfair to the weak. In his reading, the gods over the nations became *corrupt*. They did not rule well. Heiser read the Bible as treating these gods as spirit beings, not only as statues of wood and stone.

words.d: a Hebrew word for God or for other spirit beings; Heiser said it names beings who live in the spirit world
turned bad; no longer doing what is right

look.title: Heiser's Idea in Plain Words
look.text: After Babel, God let the nations go their own way. He set them under lesser spirit beings, the sons of God. He kept Israel for himself. Later, he planned to win the nations back.
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015); his idea described in our own words, not quoted
look.prompt: Which Bible passages from this chapter did Heiser use to build this idea?

check.q: In Heiser's reading, who did God put over the nations after Babel?
choices: Lesser elohim, the sons of God
check.why: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8 to say God set the nations under the sons of God, lesser elohim in his council.

check.q: What did Heiser say the word elohim tells about a being?
choices: That it is equal to God
That it is a human judge
That it lives in the spirit world
check.why: Heiser said elohim tells where a being lives, the spirit world, not that it is equal to Israel's God.

check.q: Which psalm did Heiser use to show God judging the elohim?
check.why: In Psalm 82, God judges the elohim for being unfair to the weak.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Read It
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 4:19–20 fits Heiser's reading, while many Jewish and Christian readers follow sons of Israel or see guardian angels.
reading: Heiser also used Deuteronomy 4:19–20. There Moses warns Israel not to worship the sun, moon and stars, the *host of heaven*. He says the LORD gave these to all the nations. But the LORD took Israel out of Egypt to be his own people. Heiser saw the same pattern as in Deuteronomy 32.

Not everyone reads it this way. Rashi was a famous Jewish teacher in France who died in 1105. He followed sons of Israel. He linked the seventy nations to the seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Many Christian readers have also kept sons of Israel.

Other Jewish and Christian readers follow sons of God but read them as *guardian angels*. In this view, each nation has an angel who watches over it. The book of Daniel speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece (Daniel 10:20). All these readers agree the verse is about God and the nations. They differ on who the sons are.

words.d: the sun, moon and stars; in some verses, also the heavenly beings around God
angels that some readers believe watch over a person or a nation

look.title: Three Readings Side by Side
look.text: Deuteronomy 32:8, by the number of ______. Reading 1 (Masoretic Text, Rashi): sons of Israel, like the seventy of Jacob's family. Reading 2 (Heiser): sons of God, lesser elohim who ruled the nations and became corrupt. Reading 3 (some other readers): sons of God, angels who guard the nations.
look.prompt: What do all three readings agree on? Where do they differ?

check.q: In Deuteronomy 4:19, what does Moses warn Israel not to worship?
check.why: Deuteronomy 4:19 warns against worshiping the sun, moon and stars, the host of heaven.

check.q: How did Rashi explain sons of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: As the angels of the nations
As the seventy of Jacob's family who went to Egypt
check.why: Rashi linked the seventy nations to the seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt.

check.q: What does Daniel 10:20 mention?
choices: A prince of Persia and a prince of Greece
check.why: Daniel 10:20 speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece, which some readers take as angels over nations.

review.q: In Genesis 11, what did the builders want to build?
choices: A city and a tower reaching toward the sky
review.why: Genesis 11:4 says the people planned a city and a tower whose top reached into the sky.

review.q: Heiser called Babel which rebellion in Genesis?
review.why: Heiser counted Eden first, Genesis 6 second and Babel third.
Genesis 10 lists the peoples who came from Noah's sons, so it is called the Table of Nations.

review.q: Why is the number seventy important in this chapter?
choices: It is Noah's age at the flood
It is the number of psalms
It is the usual count of nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10
It is the number of bricks in the tower
review.why: Readers count seventy nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10, and seventy came to stand for all nations.

review.q: Which old copy says sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: A Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy
review.why: A Dead Sea Scroll copy of Deuteronomy says sons of God. The Masoretic Text and the King James say sons of Israel.

review.q: What does Deuteronomy 32:9 say is the LORD's portion?
review.why: Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob.

review.q: Which reader followed sons of Israel and linked it to Jacob's family of seventy?
review.why: Rashi, a Jewish teacher in France, linked the verse to the seventy of Jacob's family who went to Egypt.

review.q: How is Heiser's reading different from the guardian angel reading?
choices: Heiser saw the sons of God as lesser elohim who became corrupt rulers
Heiser said there were no nations
Heiser said Babel did not matter
review.why: Both readings follow sons of God, but Heiser saw them as lesser elohim who ruled the nations badly, as in Psalm 82.
